tagline.text: A roughly 60 m "Big Falls" reached by stairs down through Sagada's rice terraces

location.label: Location
location.text: Near Barangay Bangaan, Sagada, Mountain Province

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,500 (estimate for one group of 1–7 people, including guide and vehicle)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Reached overland from Baguio or Tuguegarao side (Sagada has no airport); departing from Manila (MNL)

children.text: Bomod-ok Falls is a waterfall about 60 m high that you reach by walking down stone stairs past Kankanaey villages and rice terraces in Sagada. The name means "big falls," and a guide is mandatory.

Bomod-ok Falls lies southeast of Sagada in Mountain Province, at the end of a path that drops down the mountainside past Bangaan village and the Fidelisan rice terraces. "Bomod-ok" is said to mean "big" in the local Kankanaey language, which is why the place is also called Big Falls in English. Sources disagree on the height, giving roughly 40–60 m, or about 200 feet (around 60 m), and it is a single, straight drop. What makes this waterfall special on a Sagada trip is as much the walk as the fall itself. No road reaches the falls, so you have to walk down stairs of stone and concrete and along narrow paddy dikes. The path follows terraces that Kankanaey families still farm today, and the falls' water is said to supply the village with drinking and irrigation water. Remember that this is a place where people live before it is a tourist attraction, and walk accordingly.

There are two main approaches. One starts at Aguid and passes Pide and Fidelisan; it is described as a moderate route of about 5 km round trip with roughly 250 m of climbing, taking around 1.5–2 hours. The other goes straight down from the Bangaan entrance, about 4.2 km round trip with roughly 340 m of climbing, and is rated harder because the stairs never let up. Either way, the descent takes about 30 minutes to 1 hour, and the climb back is the hardest part. Under Sagada's tourism rules and village regulations a guide is mandatory, so register at the tourism office before you set out and arrange a guide there. There is a deep pool in front of the falls where you can swim, but the water is very cold all year, and some visitors report temperatures below 15 degrees in the rainy season. The falls combine well with Sumaguing Cave or the Kiltepan sunrise in a Sagada itinerary, and if you are fit you can finish in half a day. However, there were reports that the falls were closed temporarily in July 2025 for a local observance, so check with the Sagada tourism office on the current situation before you go.

First-time visitors often ask which route to take. The route straight down from Bangaan is shorter but the stairs are relentless and hard on the knees, while the route from Aguid through Fidelisan is longer but spends more time on the paddy dikes, and many reviewers prefer it for the scenery. Which path you take depends on the guide's advice and village conditions that day, so mention your preference when you register but follow your guide's judgment. Sagada manages its caves and waterfalls through a guide system. The guide does more than show the way: guides help visitors respect local customs and stay out of restricted areas, and fees are often charged per group rather than per person, so teaming up with other travelers lowers the cost. Rules change from year to year and sources disagree, so rather than memorizing numbers, check the current rates at the tourism office on the day.

The most common comment about the physical side is that the climb back is far harder than the moment you see the falls. Going down you have time to take photos, but coming up you climb the steps one by one in the sun, and they are slipperier after rain. Rest often, drink plenty of water, and do not linger so long at the falls that you get chilled. If you rarely exercise, allow generous time and ask your guide to match your pace.

Depending on the source the height is given as about 40–60 m, and the water falls in one straight drop. In the rainy season the flow thickens and spray spreads like mist. The spray soaks camera lenses quickly near the base, so bring a waterproof pouch.

blocks.title: A Path Through the Rice Terraces

children.text: Kankanaey rice terraces unfold all along the way down. The dikes are narrow and the stone walls steep, so watch your footing and walk slowly. Access can be blocked during planting and harvest, so ask your guide in advance.

blocks.title: Swimming in the Cold Plunge Pool

children.text: The pool below the falls may be deep, so assume it is deep unless your guide says otherwise. If you are not a confident swimmer, the shallower sections downstream are safer. There are no changing rooms, so you change behind rocks or climb back up wet.

blocks.title: Hidden Small Falls and Rock Passages

children.text: Around the main falls there are smaller cascades reached through low gaps in the rock. The footing is slippery, so you need shoes with good grip. Slippers are not recommended.

The path runs between Kankanaey communities. When photographing people, especially elders and children, ask permission first, and never step into planted paddies or irrigation channels. Carry all your trash out.

blocks.title: Easy to Combine with a Sagada Itinerary

children.text: You go from Sagada town by vehicle to the starting point at Bangaan or Aguid. Seeing the falls in the morning and visiting a place like Sumaguing Cave in the afternoon is possible, but the climb back takes a lot of energy.

A guide leads the way under the rules set by the village and the tourism office. The path is narrow and steep and the mobile signal is weak, so following your guide's pace and instructions is safest, and it also supports local livelihoods.

items.title: Half-Day Course
items.subtitle: Round trip from Bangaan to the falls

children.text: Register at the tourism office in Sagada town and pay the environmental and tourism fee. You may be asked for the receipt on site, so keep it.
Travel with your guide by vehicle to the starting point at Bangaan (or Aguid).
Walk down the stairs and along the paddy dikes. It takes about 30 minutes to 1 hour.
Arrive at the falls for photos and a swim. The water is cold, so do not stay too long.
Climb back up slowly. Allow at least about 1 hour.
Return to town for lunch.
Timings assume an ordinary walking pace and vary with weather and fitness.

items.title: Sagada Day Course
items.subtitle: The falls plus a stroll through town

children.text: Sunrise spots such as Kiltepan have set times, so ask your accommodation the day before.
Register at the tourism office, find a guide, and head to Bangaan.
Walk down to the falls, take photos and swim, then climb back up.
Return to town, have lunch, and rest to recover your strength.
If you still have energy, take an easy walk around town and relax.
Adding a cave on the same day makes the schedule very tight, so we recommend one attraction per day.

items.title: From Sagada to the Starting Point

children.text: From Sagada town you hire a vehicle to Bangaan or Aguid. A 2019 review quoted about
round trip, but check the current rate at the tourism office.
From there you reach the falls only on foot. No road reaches the falls.

Some guides say November to February is relatively cool and dry and good for walking, while others call November to April the dry season. The terraces are said to be especially beautiful in April–May and at harvest time, though the timing varies from year to year.
August to October brings heavy monsoon rain, a higher risk of landslides, and very slippery stairs and rocks. On rainy days it is safer to talk with your guide and change your plans.

Accommodation is concentrated in Sagada town. Because you travel by vehicle from town to Bangaan or Aguid, staying in town is the most convenient. Book early in peak season.
Lunch in town after the trek is the usual plan. There is no restaurant at the falls, so bring water and snacks and carry your trash out.
Sagada is high up and cool in the mornings and evenings, so bring a warm layer. If you went into the cold water, change out of wet clothes right away.

There are no shops or restaurants around the falls, so prepare simple snacks and energy bars in town before setting out. You may come back late from the trek, so ask your accommodation about a place for dinner in advance.
Wear trekking shoes or sandals with good grip and avoid smooth slippers.
Bring spare clothes, a small towel, and a waterproof pouch. There are no changing rooms.
Bring your own water and snacks.
Allow plenty of time for the climb back and start up before it gets late.
Guide fees are charged per group, so sharing with other travelers lowers the cost.
Carry enough cash. Card payment may be difficult outside town.
Mobile signal is weak or absent, so follow your guide for directions.
Register through the
Sagada municipal tourism office

before departure. Ask the accredited local guides’ association (BFTAMPGA, +63 935 353 8169 / +63 905 883 2870) about access, guide fees and group limits. Community ubaya closures and heavy rain can disrupt visits.
A trekking pole or light walking stick helps if you have bad knees.
A guide is mandatory and the falls may close for village events or farming seasons, so confirm with the Sagada tourism office before you go.
The pool may be deep, so swim only where your guide says it is safe.
The stairs and rocks are very slippery after rain.
The falls' water serves the village, so do not use soap or shampoo and leave no trash.
Do not step into the paddies or block the channels, and ask permission before photographing people.
Check the latest notices for fees and rules.
The Bangaan and Fidelisan area is a living village, so avoid loud noise, drone filming, and pushy photo requests. Use a drone only after checking local rules.
The town you drive from to the trailhead, with accommodation, restaurants, and the tourism office. Caves and sunrise spots are nearby.
